title: Create a list of `EmployeeDTO(name, department)` from the employee list using `map()`.
shortTitle: Create a list of EmployeeDTO(name, department) from the employee list using map()
keyPoints: map() can transform one object type to another, constructing a new DTO per element
DTO (Data Transfer Object) carries only the fields a particular layer needs, decoupling internal models from APIs
The mapping function constructs the DTO: e -> new EmployeeDTO(e.getName(), e.getDepartment())
Sensitive fields like salary are excluded by design because the mapping function never reads them
In Spring applications, the map step is where entity-to-DTO conversion happens before the API response
For large projects, mapping libraries like MapStruct generate the boilerplate, but understanding manual map is essential

s1_definition.oneliner: `map` can build a new, slimmer object per element, exposing only the fields a layer should see.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Object-to-object map**: projects a rich domain entity into a slimmer Data Transfer Object.
- **DTO purpose**: carries only the fields a particular layer needs, no business logic.
- **Decoupling**: changing a database column does not break the API when DTOs sit between them.
- **Security**: sensitive fields like salary are excluded because the mapping function never reads them.
- **Spring pattern**: controllers return DTOs, never entities, to prevent lazy-loading issues and data leaks.
s1_definition.analogy: The HR system at the National Bank of India holds a full employee file with salary, address, and bank details, but the public staff webpage should only show name and department. A clerk copies just those two fields onto a simpler summary card for each person. That summary card is the DTO.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Employee (rich entity)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ name: "Rajesh"                   │
  │ department: "Loans"              │
  │ salary: 95000  ← NOT copied     │
  │ address: "..." ← NOT copied     │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘
       │
       │  map(e -> new EmployeeDTO(name, dept))
       ▼
  EmployeeDTO (slim transfer object)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ name: "Rajesh"                   │
  │ department: "Loans"              │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘
  Salary never read → never exposed
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To project a rich entity into a slimmer transfer object I use map, where the mapping function constructs a new DTO from only the fields I want to expose. For each employee I built an EmployeeDTO carrying just name and department, so every employee became exactly one DTO, one-to-one, and I collected the result into a list. The salary was simply never read, so it could not appear in the output.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was the public staff directory on the intranet. The internal employee record contains salary and other sensitive fields that must never reach that page, so the map step was the deliberate point where I narrowed the full entity down to the two safe fields.

The DTO pattern matters because it decouples the internal model from the external contract, keeps sensitive data from leaking, and shapes the response to exactly what the view needs. In Spring applications I keep controllers returning DTOs and never entities, and on larger projects I use MapStruct, but I always understand the manual map first.

Remember one sentence: `map(e -> new EmployeeDTO(name, dept))` projects each entity to a slim DTO, exposing only the fields the API should see.
